knsThemes.title: Geography and water
knsThemes.prompt: What do you know about the Netherlands and water? Think of: below sea level, dikes, provinces, capital.
knsThemes.body: The Netherlands is small, flat and busy: about 18 million people. Roughly a quarter of the land lies below sea level, so dikes, dunes and pumping stations keep the water out. After the big flood of 1953 the Delta Works were built in the south-west. There are 12 provinces. Amsterdam is the capital, but the government and parliament sit in The Hague (Den Haag). Rotterdam has one of the biggest ports in the world.
knsThemes.words: de dijk (dike) · de zee (sea) · de provincie (province) · de hoofdstad (capital)

knsThemes.title: How the country is governed
knsThemes.prompt: Who has political power: the King or the government? What is the Tweede Kamer?
knsThemes.body: The Netherlands is a constitutional monarchy and a parliamentary democracy. The King is head of state, but ministers carry the political responsibility. The government is led by the prime minister (minister-president). Parliament (de Staten-Generaal) has two chambers; the Tweede Kamer has 150 members, elected at least every four years. Many parties take part, so governments are usually coalitions. Locally, each municipality (gemeente) has an elected council and a mayor (burgemeester). You can vote from age 18.
knsThemes.words: de regering (government) · de verkiezingen (elections) · stemmen (to vote) · de gemeente (municipality)

knsThemes.title: The royal family
knsThemes.prompt: Who is the King? Which day is King's Day and what colour do people wear?
knsThemes.body: King Willem-Alexander has been king since 2013. Queen Máxima is his wife, and their eldest daughter, Princess Amalia, is next in line. The family belongs to the House of Orange, which is why orange is the national colour. On King's Day (Koningsdag, 27 April) people wear orange and many towns have street markets. On Prinsjesdag (the third Tuesday of September) the King reads out the government's plans for the coming year.
knsThemes.words: de koning (king) · de koningin (queen) · Koningsdag (King's Day) · oranje (orange)

knsThemes.title: History
knsThemes.prompt: What was the Golden Age? What happened in 1940–1945? What do 4 and 5 May mean?
knsThemes.body: In the 17th century (the Golden Age) the Netherlands became rich through trade and shipping; painters like Rembrandt worked then. Part of that wealth came from colonies and slavery; slavery was abolished in 1863 and is remembered on Keti Koti (1 July). In the Second World War Germany occupied the Netherlands from 1940 to 1945; Anne Frank's diary is from this time. On 4 May the war dead are remembered with two minutes of silence, and 5 May is Liberation Day. After the war people came from Indonesia, Suriname, Turkey, Morocco and elsewhere.
knsThemes.words: de oorlog (war) · de bevrijding (liberation) · herdenken (to commemorate)

knsThemes.title: Manners and social customs
knsThemes.prompt: How do Dutch people greet, make plans and celebrate birthdays?
knsThemes.body: People usually shake hands when they meet someone new and introduce themselves by name. Being on time matters, and people plan visits in advance (even with friends and family). Dutch people are often direct: they say what they think, which is not meant to be rude. Use 'u' for strangers, officials and older people, and 'je/jij' for friends. At a birthday party you congratulate not only the person with the birthday but also their family ('Gefeliciteerd!').
knsThemes.words: de afspraak (appointment) · op tijd (on time) · gefeliciteerd (congratulations) · u / jij (you, formal / informal)

knsThemes.title: Education
knsThemes.prompt: From what age must children go to school? What comes after primary school?
knsThemes.body: Children must go to school from age 5 (most start at 4). Primary school (basisschool) has 8 groups. After that pupils go to secondary school at different levels: vmbo (practical), havo, or vwo (pre-university). Then they can continue at mbo, hbo or university. Young people must keep learning until 18 or until they have a basic diploma. Parents are expected to be involved, for example at parents' evenings.
knsThemes.words: de basisschool (primary school) · de leerplicht (compulsory education) · het diploma (diploma) · de ouders (parents)

knsThemes.title: Health care
knsThemes.prompt: Who do you go to first when you are ill? What number do you call in an emergency?
knsThemes.body: Everyone who lives and works in the Netherlands must have basic health insurance. You register with a GP (huisarts) near your home; the GP is your first stop when you are ill and refers you to a hospital or specialist if needed. Medicine is collected at the pharmacy (apotheek). In an emergency, call 112. Babies and young children have regular check-ups at the consultatiebureau.
knsThemes.words: de huisarts (GP) · de zorgverzekering (health insurance) · de apotheek (pharmacy) · 112 (emergency number)

knsThemes.title: Work and income
knsThemes.prompt: What is normal at work in the Netherlands? Who works, and what about taxes?
knsThemes.body: Men and women both work, and many people work part-time. You need a contract and you pay income tax to the Belastingdienst. There is a legal minimum wage, and employers must treat everyone equally. If you lose your job you may get unemployment benefit for a time, and older people receive a state pension (AOW). Being on time and calling in sick in the morning are expected. Many people also do volunteer work (vrijwilligerswerk).
knsThemes.words: de baan (job) · het salaris (salary) · de belasting (tax) · ziek melden (call in sick)

knsThemes.title: Fundamental rights
knsThemes.prompt: What does Article 1 of the Constitution say? Can two men or two women marry?
knsThemes.body: Article 1 of the Dutch Constitution says everyone must be treated equally in equal cases; discrimination is not allowed (for example because of religion, gender, race or sexual orientation). People are free to choose their religion, and church and state are separate. Freedom of speech is protected, as long as you do not break the law. Men and women have equal rights, and two people of the same sex can marry (the Netherlands was the first country to allow this, in 2001).
knsThemes.words: de grondwet (constitution) · gelijk (equal) · de vrijheid (freedom) · discriminatie (discrimination)

knsThemes.title: Living there and integrating
knsThemes.prompt: What do you do first after moving? What happens after the exam abroad?
knsThemes.body: After arriving you register at the municipality (gemeente) and receive a citizen service number (BSN), which you need for work, the doctor and the bank. Most newcomers then follow a civic integration course and take further exams in the Netherlands (inburgering). Most people rent their home; waste is separated (paper, glass, plastic) and collected on set days. Neighbours greet each other, and it is normal to introduce yourself when you move in.
knsThemes.words: inschrijven (to register) · het BSN (citizen service number) · de inburgering (civic integration) · de buren (neighbours)
